title: The 2026 international student planning level of 295,000 is not legally enforceable; it works through visa-processing slow lanes because the Senate rejected formal caps in 2024
oneLiner: The lever a migration cap would pull is an administrative one, not a law.
body: After the Senate blocked legislated caps in November 2024, the government set 'national planning levels' for new international students and enforced them by slowing visa processing once a provider reaches 80 per cent of its allocation. The level rose from 270,000 in 2025 to 295,000 in 2026, with the Australian Tertiary Education Commission due to take over regulation of higher-education numbers from 2027.
contextBackground: How student numbers are actually controlled bears on whether a hard net-migration cap could be delivered at all, and on who would bear it.
contextDisagreement: Agreed as a description. Disputed is whether soft caps are a workable substitute for a legislated number or an invitation to miss it.

evidenceItems.citation: The Conversation, Andrew Norton, 5 August 2025 — planning levels, enforceability and the 2027 commission

otherClaim.title: Holding net overseas migration below 200,000 would require large cuts to international student numbers

claimItself.title: Holding net overseas migration below 200,000 would require large cuts to international student numbers
claimItself.oneLiner: Students are the biggest component of net migration, so a cap of this size is mostly a cap on them.
claimItself.body: Permanent skilled and family visas are already capped and make up a minority of net migration. The remainder is dominated by students, with working-holiday makers and temporary skilled workers behind them. Holding the total below 200,000 while keeping the permanent program at current levels leaves international education as the only component large enough to cut.
